sections.title: What Makes a Strong Argument?
sections.content: A strong argument is more than just an opinion — it is a structured claim supported by reasoning and evidence. The AREST framework gives you a five-component formula for building arguments that hold up under scrutiny.
bullets: A — Assertion: Your main claim or position
R — Reasoning: Why your assertion is true
E — Evidence: The facts or data that support your reasoning
S — Significance: Why this argument matters in the bigger picture
T — Tie-back: How this connects back to the overall debate motion

sections.title: Breaking Down Each Component
sections.content: Let's examine each part of AREST in detail. The Assertion is your one-sentence claim — clear and debatable. Reasoning explains the logic connecting your evidence to your claim. Evidence provides concrete support — statistics, examples, expert testimony. Significance tells the audience why this point matters. The Tie-back explicitly connects your argument back to the debate motion.
bullets: Assertion: 'Schools should start at 9 AM' — specific and debatable
Reasoning: 'Teenagers have biological sleep cycles that make early starts counterproductive'
Evidence: 'A 2023 study in the Journal of Adolescent Health found a 15% GPA increase in schools starting at 9 AM'
Significance: 'This affects millions of students' academic performance and wellbeing'
Tie-back: 'Therefore, this motion to reform school hours is supported by both science and outcomes'

sections.title: AREST in Action
sections.content: Let's break down a full argument using AREST.
sections.good:
Assertion: Social media companies should be held legally responsible for misinformation on their platforms.
Reasoning: Current moderation practices are reactive, not preventive, allowing viral falsehoods to spread before they are removed.
Evidence: A Stanford study found false news spreads six times faster than true news on Twitter.
Significance: Misinformation erodes democratic processes and public health — the cost of inaction is unacceptable.
Tie-back: This directly supports the motion that tech companies must be regulated for content accuracy.
sections.bad: Social media is bad and should be stopped because there is too much fake news.
sections.explanation: The good argument uses all five AREST components to build a complete, persuasive case. The bad argument makes an assertion without reasoning, evidence, or significance — it is just an opinion.

sections.instruction: Which component of AREST answers the question 'So what?'
sections.feedback: Significance explains why your argument matters and why the audience should care — it answers 'So what?'

sections.feedback: AREST builds a complete argument: start with your claim, justify it with logic, prove it with facts, explain its importance, and connect it to the big picture.

sections.q: What is the difference between Reasoning and Evidence in AREST?
options: They are the same thing expressed differently
Reasoning is the logical explanation; Evidence is the factual proof
Reasoning comes after Evidence in the structure
Evidence is optional but Reasoning is required
sections.explain: Reasoning is the 'why' — the logical connection. Evidence is the 'proof' — the concrete facts that back up your reasoning.
